title: "Connecting cascade amplitudes to Dalitz-plot decomposition"
engine: julia
format:
  gfm: default
execute:
  echo: true
  output: false
---

CascadeDecays (CD) follows helicity frames through each decay vertex.
ThreeBodyDecays (TBD) factors out the orientation of a planar three-body event
and aligns its spins with real Wigner small-$d$ matrices. They describe the same
amplitude once the external spin bases, a continuous phase, and a discrete
chain sign are matched.

This page gives the conversion first, explains where its angles and signs come
from, then checks it component by component on sampled four-vectors. It follows
[Quantization reference frames in ThreeBodyDecays](https://github.com/mmikhasenko/ThreeBodyDecays.jl/blob/main/docs/src/11-quantization-reference.md).
For spin-zero daughters, see also [the COMPASS example](compass-basis.md).

## The relation to use

Write $k$ for the chain topology and $r=\mathtt{reference\_k}$ for the common
quantization reference. Keep the cyclic daughter order:

| Index | Topology | Isobar daughters | Spectator |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 1 | $(23)1$ | $(2,3)$ | 1 |
| 2 | $(31)2$ | $(3,1)$ | 2 |
| 3 | $(12)3$ | $(1,2)$ | 3 |

For matched vertex conventions, LS couplings, particle-2 phases, normalization,
and line shapes, the full complex tensors obey

$$
\boxed{
A_{\mathrm{CD},\boldsymbol\lambda,m_0}^{k;r}
=S(k,r)\,e^{i\lambda_r\gamma_r}
 A_{\mathrm{TBD},\boldsymbol\lambda,m_0}^{k;r}}
$$

Here $\boldsymbol\lambda=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)$ are helicities in the
**reference** frames, $m_0$ is the parent projection in the external frame, and
$\gamma_r$ is the inner azimuth of the **reference** chain. Physical helicities
appear in the exponential; Julia's `two_js` and `two_λ` values must be divided
by two. Both tensors use axes `(λ1, λ2, λ3, m0)`.

The sign is particularly simple:

$$
S(k,r)=\begin{cases}
1,& k=r,\\
(-1)^{2j_\ell},&\ell=6-k-r\quad(k\ne r).
\end{cases}
$$

Thus only the spin of the particle **absent from the pair $(k,r)$** matters.
An integer spin gives $+1$; a half-integer spin gives $-1$.

| Chain $k$ / reference $r$ | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 1 | $1$ | $(-1)^{2j_3}$ | $(-1)^{2j_2}$ |
| 2 | $(-1)^{2j_3}$ | $1$ | $(-1)^{2j_1}$ |
| 3 | $(-1)^{2j_2}$ | $(-1)^{2j_1}$ | $1$ |

For example, comparing chain $(12)3$ with reference $(23)1$ means $k=3,r=1$:
$A_{\rm CD}^{3;1}=(-1)^{2j_2}e^{i\lambda_1\gamma_1}A_{\rm TBD}^{3;1}$.
The sign is set by particle 2, while the continuous phase uses particle 1.
Neither is determined by the parent spin alone.

## Which angles are we comparing?

Work in the parent rest frame, with massive daughters and a nondegenerate
event. Momentum conservation puts the three momenta in one plane. The canonical
reference event has the isobar along $+z$, spectator $r$ along $-z$, and the
cyclic first daughter in the positive-$x$ half-plane. Its normal is $+y$.

The three orientation angles rotate this canonical event into the supplied
four-vectors:

$$
R(\Omega_r)=R_z(\alpha_r)R_y(\beta_r)R_z(\gamma_r).
$$

To obtain them, follow the reference chain: $(\alpha_r,\beta_r)$ orient its
isobar in the parent frame; after going into that isobar's helicity frame,
the first daughter's azimuth is $\gamma_r$. In the compatibility helper this
is `reference_plane_orientation(three_body_topology(r), objs)` and the result
is `(α, cosβ, γ)`. Use the same $r$ for this operation and for TBD evaluation.
The overall orientation rotates the parent index with $D^{j_0*}(\Omega_r)$.

There are three different kinds of angles here:

| Angles | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| $\Omega_r=(\alpha_r,\beta_r,\gamma_r)$ | Orient the reference event relative to external axes. |
| $\theta_{ij}$ | Describe the inner two-body decay in chain $k$. |
| $\zeta^a_{k(r)}$ | Align leg $a$ of chain $k$ with reference $r$ in the canonical plane. |

TBD's internal alignments are pure $y$ rotations. Obtain their **signed** angles
from `cosζ(wr(k,r,a), σs, ms^2)` and `ispositive(wr(k,r,a))`, not from `acos`
alone. CD instead follows a rotation and boost at each vertex, so comparisons
between its local frames generally produce full Euler triples. Those extra
Euler angles describe the local axes and their rotation paths; they are not
additional independent kinematic variables or a nonplanar decay.

## Why the spectator phase remains

Fix the Wigner convention

$$
D^j_{mn}(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)
=e^{-im\alpha}d^j_{mn}(\beta)e^{-in\gamma}.
$$

The reference cascade $0\to R+r$, $R\to i+j$ contains

$$
D^{j_0*}_{m_0,\lambda_R-\lambda_r}(\alpha_r,\beta_r,0)
D^{j_R*}_{\lambda_R,\lambda_i-\lambda_j}(\gamma_r,\theta_{ij},0).
$$

The second factor contributes $e^{+i\lambda_R\gamma_r}$: the plus sign follows
from complex conjugation. Moving the inner azimuth into the third Euler angle
of the parent factor contributes $e^{+i(\lambda_R-\lambda_r)\gamma_r}$.
Their ratio is therefore $e^{+i\lambda_r\gamma_r}$, giving

$$
\begin{aligned}
&D^{j_0*}_{m_0,\lambda_R-\lambda_r}(\alpha_r,\beta_r,0)
D^{j_R*}_{\lambda_R,\lambda_i-\lambda_j}(\gamma_r,\theta_{ij},0)\\
&\quad=D^{j_0*}_{m_0,\lambda_R-\lambda_r}(\Omega_r)
e^{i\lambda_r\gamma_r}
 d^{j_R}_{\lambda_R,\lambda_i-\lambda_j}(\theta_{ij}).
\end{aligned}
$$

TBD includes the overall $D^*$ but does not include this remaining spectator
phase. At fixed reference and external helicities, the phase is common to all
chains. Do not substitute the spectator or inner azimuth of each target chain.

## Where the minus signs come from

A spatial rotation does not uniquely specify its action on a spinor: a full
turn leaves spatial axes unchanged but multiplies spin $j$ by $(-1)^{2j}$.
Two distinctions prevent most sign mistakes.

First, a negative planar angle may be written using positive middle Euler angle:

$$
R_y(-\theta)=R_z(\pi)R_y(\theta)R_z(-\pi).
$$

This identity is exact for spinors and adds **no** sign. Replacing the last
$-\pi$ by $+\pi$, however, adds a full turn:

$$
D^j(\pi,\theta,\pi)=(-1)^{2j}d^j(-\theta).
$$

Second, TBD uses direct principal signed angles in $[-\pi,\pi]$. The positive
cyclic parent angles sum to $2\pi$, so composing two pairwise alignments can
differ from the direct third alignment by a full turn. CD's vertex paths can
also reverse and restore local plane normals through azimuthal $\pi$ rotations.
Compare the spin matrices, not just their spatial axes or Euler angles modulo
$2\pi$.

A way to **compute**, rather than guess, the residual signs is to compare the
frame maps in the spin-$1/2$ representation. Define the diagonal spectator phase
$P_a(q)_{mm'}=\delta_{mm'}e^{im\gamma_q\delta_{aq}}$, and let $C_a(k\leftarrow r)$
be CD's conjugated final-leg Wigner matrix, with rows in the chain frame and
columns in the reference frame. With the same index order for TBD's $d_a(k,r)$,
compare the two sides of

$$
\begin{aligned}
D^{j_0*}(\Omega_k)&=\epsilon_0^{2j_0}D^{j_0*}(\Omega_r)d_0(k,r),\\
P_a(k)C_a(k\leftarrow r)&=\epsilon_a^{2j_a}d_a(k,r)P_a(r).
\end{aligned}
$$

At spin $1/2$, form $L R^\dagger$ from each pair of matrices before inserting
$\epsilon_a$. It must be $+I$ or $-I$, which gives $\epsilon_a$ directly. A
noncentral residual is a mismatch of conventions or kinematics, not a sign
that can be repaired by choosing $\pm1$.

The full amplitude sign is $\epsilon_0^{2j_0}\prod_a\epsilon_a^{2j_a}$.
Allowed angular-momentum couplings obey
$2j_0=2j_1+2j_2+2j_3\pmod 2$, so introduce $q_a=\epsilon_0\epsilon_a$:

$$
S(k,r)=\prod_{a=1}^3q_a^{2j_a}.
$$

The cyclic paths give $q_a=-1$ only for the particle absent from $(k,r)$;
for $k=r$ all are $+1$. This gives the sign table above, for any allowed
spin magnitudes and LS couplings. Individual $\epsilon_a$ assignments can
change with Euler branches; the reduced rule keeps the complete chain sign.

## Brute-force check on four-vectors

A comparison of intensities alone would miss both a common phase and an
overall chain sign. The executable check below compares **every complex tensor
component** against the predicted relation, without fitting a phase or choosing
the better of $+A$ and $-A$.

The [validation script](https://github.com/RUB-EP1/CascadeDecays.jl/blob/main/docs/checks/cascade-dpd.jl)
keeps the implementation out of the derivation. It:

- samples interior Dalitz points and independently rotates their four-vectors;
- exercises all three chains and all three reference choices;
- includes scalar, integer-spin and half-integer-spin cases, including two and
  three fermions and spin $3/2$;
- enumerates every allowed LS pair for two isobar-spin choices per case, passing
  identical couplings to both libraries;
- asserts the predicted relation with absolute and relative tolerances, and
  verifies that omitting either the phase or sign produces a detectable error.

The masses are those of $\Lambda_c\to pK\pi$, but the spin assignments are toy
systems. Unit line shapes isolate the angular convention. The finite sample is
an executable stress test of the general relation, not a proof for all spins.
Exact Euler poles and degenerate phase-space boundaries require a shared
limiting-frame prescription and are excluded here.

```{julia}
#| label: validate-general-relation
#| output: true
include(joinpath(@__DIR__, "checks", "cascade-dpd.jl"))
result = validate_conversion()
print_validation(result)
```

Run more samples independently with:

```julia
include("docs/checks/cascade-dpd.jl")
print_validation(validate_conversion(nsamples = 100, seed = 42))
```

The `cases` keyword accepts `(final doubled spins, parent doubled spin)` pairs,
for example `((3,1,0),2)`. For each case the isobar doubled spins are
`two_js[i] + two_js[j]` and that value plus two; forbidden vertex assignments
are skipped. The default run checks all nine topology pairs and requires
nontrivial phase and sign witnesses. A failed comparison reports the seed,
event, spins, chain, reference, LS couplings and residual.

Evaluate TBD with `amplitude(chain, po, σs; reference_k=r)` using the
[documentation environment](https://github.com/RUB-EP1/CascadeDecays.jl/blob/main/docs/README.md).
The component-wise check includes the spin-1 spectator / scalar-isobar case,
so it also detects omitted helicity components rather than mistaking them for
an additional phase or sign.

## Using the relation in a coherent model

At fixed reference, convert each CD coefficient using
$c_{\mathrm{TBD},n}^{(r)}=S(k_n,r)c_{\mathrm{CD},n}$. The spectator phase is
common to all terms at fixed external helicities and cancels from unpolarized
intensities. Keep it when comparing amplitudes or spin-density information.

Changing a TBD model's reference from $r$ to $s$ also requires

$$
c_{\mathrm{TBD},n}^{(s)}
=S(k_n,s)S(k_n,r)c_{\mathrm{TBD},n}^{(r)}.
$$

Transform the external spin bases as well when comparing tensors. Changing
only `reference_k` while keeping numerical coefficients can change
interference. Store the reference with the fitted couplings.
